Frontend Development for DApps

Connect wallets, fetch balances, and send transactions safely using ethers.js. Practical patterns and common pitfalls included.

screens.title: Provider vs Signer
screens.narratorSegment: Two concepts you will use constantly are provider and signer. A provider is an abstraction that allows your DApp to read blockchain data: block numbers, balances, and logs. It does not sign transactions. A signer, by contrast, represents an account with the ability to sign transactions and messages; it typically wraps a user's wallet account once the user grants access. For example, provider. getBalance(address) queries the chain for a balance, whereas signer. sendTransaction(transaction) asks the wallet to sign and broadcast a state-changing transaction. Confusing these leads to common mistakes: calling sendTransaction on a provider does nothing, and trying to fetch private data from a signer is not its purpose. Practically, you create a BrowserProvider from window. ethereum, then call provider. getSigner() to obtain the signer for the connected account. This separation improves safety because read operations can be performed using public RPC providers like Infura when necessary, while signing always requires explicit user consent in their wallet. Remember: queries use the provider, state changes require the signer. Provider vs Signer means provider = read-only queries. signer = signing capability and sending transactions on behalf of the user.. In practical terms, understanding the roles: query vs sign. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › Provider vs Signer
Definition
Provider

An interface for querying chain data. Use it to get balances, block info, and read-only contract state. Example: provider.getBalance(address).

Signer

Represents an account able to sign transactions and messages. It prompts the user through their wallet for consent before sending transactions.

Contrast & examples
  • Use provider.getBalance(address) to read a balance without user prompts.
  • Use signer.sendTransaction({ to, value }) to request the wallet sign and broadcast a transfer.
  • Use public RPC providers for heavy read work; reserve signer usage for actions requiring user consent.
Key Takeaway

Keep queries and signing separate: provider for reads, signer for writes requiring explicit user approval.

screens.title: Wallet connection flow
screens.narratorSegment: Connecting a wallet follows a clear sequence that your app should implement and handle robustly. First, check for window. ethereum; if absent, instruct the user to install a compatible wallet. Second, call window. ethereum. request with the method eth_requestAccounts to prompt the user to connect. If the user approves, create a BrowserProvider from window. ethereum and obtain a signer via provider. getSigner(). Store provider and signer references, update the UI to show connected state, and enable actions like getting account info or sending transactions. Third, listen for relevant wallet events such as accountsChanged and chainChanged so the app can refresh data or prompt the user when the network changes. Always wrap the request call in try... catch to detect user rejection; a rejection typically yields an error code like 4001 and should be presented as an expected user action, not a fatal app error. This flow ensures clarity, reduces accidental transactions, and makes the app resilient to wallet state changes. content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › Connect Wallet Code
Key snippet
connectWalletBtn.addEventListener('click', async () => {
  if (typeof window.ethereum !== 'undefined') {
    try {
      await window.ethereum.request({ method: 'eth_requestAccounts' });
      provider = new ethers.BrowserProvider(window.ethereum);
      signer = await provider.getSigner();
      userAddress = await signer.getAddress();
      outputDiv.textContent = `Wallet connected: ${userAddress}
`;
      updateUI(true);
      window.ethereum.on('accountsChanged', (accounts) => { /* handle */ });
      window.ethereum.on('chainChanged', (chainId) => { window.location.reload(); });
    } catch (error) {
      outputDiv.textContent = `Error connecting wallet: ${error.message}`;
      updateUI(false);
    }
  } else {
    outputDiv.textContent = 'MetaMask not detected.';
  }
});
Explanation & best practices
  • Always check window.ethereum before calling requests to avoid exceptions.
  • Call updateUI only after provider and signer are initialized so buttons reflect true state.
  • Use event listeners to react to wallet changes rather than relying on a page refresh alone.
Misconception

Assuming a connected signer never changes. Users can switch accounts or networks at any time; always verify before sending transactions.

Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › Get Account Info
displayAccountInfo
async function displayAccountInfo() {
  if (!signer || !userAddress) {
    outputDiv.textContent += '
Wallet not connected.';
    return;
  }
  try {
    const balance = await provider.getBalance(userAddress);
    outputDiv.textContent += `
Connected Address: ${userAddress}
Balance: ${ethers.formatEther(balance)} ETH`;
  } catch (error) {
    outputDiv.textContent += `
Error displaying account info: ${error.message}`;
  }
}
Notes & pitfalls
  • formatEther converts BigInt to decimal ETH string for display.
  • Balances can be out of date if there are pending transactions; refresh after confirmations.
  • Always guard calls with signer and userAddress checks to avoid exceptions.
Key Takeaway

Fetch balance with provider.getBalance and convert with ethers.formatEther so users see readable ETH amounts.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › Send ETH
Transaction snippet
const recipientAddress = '0xYourRecipientAddressHere';
const amountToSend = ethers.parseEther('0.001');
try {
  outputDiv.textContent += `
Initiating transaction to ${recipientAddress} for ${ethers.formatEther(amountToSend)} ETH...`;
  const tx = await signer.sendTransaction({ to: recipientAddress, value: amountToSend });
  outputDiv.textContent += `
Transaction sent! Hash: ${tx.hash}`;
  outputDiv.textContent += `
Waiting for transaction to be mined...`;
  await tx.wait();
  outputDiv.textContent += `
Transaction confirmed!`;
} catch (error) {
  outputDiv.textContent += `
Error sending ETH: ${error.message}`;
  if (error.code === 4001) outputDiv.textContent += '
Transaction rejected by user.';
  if (error.code === 'INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS') outputDiv.textContent += '
Insufficient funds for gas.';
}
Guidance
  • Replace placeholder recipient addresses before sending on any network.
  • Show clear status updates during submission and confirmation so users don’t retry prematurely.
  • After confirmation, refresh balances to reflect the new state.
Common mistake

Sending without confirming network and address changes can result in lost funds or transactions on the wrong chain.

screens.title: Browser-injected vs RPC providers
screens.narratorSegment: There are two common ways a DApp connects to the chain: browser-injected providers like MetaMask and remote RPC providers like Infura, Alchemy, or QuickNode. Browser-injected providers allow user consent and signing through the wallet extension; they expose window. ethereum and are necessary for operations requiring the user’s key. RPC providers are node endpoints useful for read-only operations when you don’t need the user’s signature. A typical pattern is to use an RPC provider for heavy reads, caching, or server-side tasks, and use a BrowserProvider or injected provider only when you need to sign a transaction. Confusing these leads to UX problems: attempting to sign with an RPC provider will fail because it does not have access to a private key. On the other hand, relying exclusively on an injected provider for heavy traffic may be unreliable for some metrics or parallel requests. Plan your architecture accordingly: split read and write responsibilities based on whether a wallet signature is required. Browser-injected vs RPC providers means use injected browser providers for signing and user consent; use rpc providers for read-only operations and server-side queries.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › Provider Comparison
Browser-injected (MetaMask)
  • Requires user wallet; exposes window.ethereum.
  • Provides signer capabilities after user grants permission.
  • Best for operations where user must sign transactions.
RPC providers (Infura, Alchemy)
  • Server or client endpoints for node access without a wallet.
  • Great for read-only queries and app-level data fetching.
  • Cannot sign on behalf of the user; not a replacement for a signer.
Practical pattern

Use RPC providers for background reads and BrowserProvider for actions that require user signatures. This split reduces wallet prompts and improves performance for heavy queries.

screens.title: Handling wallet events
screens.narratorSegment: Reacting to wallet events preserves correctness in a DApp. Two events matter most: accountsChanged and chainChanged. accountsChanged fires when a user switches or disconnects accounts. If the array is empty, the user disconnected and you should clear any signer-related state and disable actions. If it contains a different address, update the stored userAddress and reinitialize the signer if necessary. chainChanged signals that the connected network changed; most apps choose to reload or reinitialize provider and signer because the chain context can change contract addresses, gas expectations, and balances. Always show a clear message so users understand why the app refreshed or why a button became disabled. Failure to handle these events leads to mistaken transactions or inconsistent UI. For example, if network mismatch is ignored, a user might unknowingly send testnet ETH while expecting mainnet behavior, or vice versa. Implement event handlers that update the UI, refresh balances, and offer guidance when a network mismatch occurs. Handling wallet events means listen and react to accountschanged and chainchanged to keep displayed data accurate and to avoid operating on the wrong account or network.. accountsChanged
Handler guidance:
  1. If accounts array is empty, clear provider, signer, and userAddress and disable actions.

chainChanged

Why it matters

Handling these events prevents mistaken transactions and keeps on-screen data accurate as users change accounts or networks in their wallet.

screens.title: Security, UX and common mistakes
screens.narratorSegment: Security and clear UX are essential in DApp frontends. First, never ask users for private keys or attempt to store them; wallets like MetaMask manage private keys securely. Second, warn users about insufficient gas and provide clear error messages when transactions fail due to funds or rejection. Third, detect network mismatches early and prevent state-changing actions when on the wrong chain. Fourth, handle promise rejections from eth_requestAccounts and signer. sendTransaction and present those rejections as possible user choices, not application failures. A common developer mistake is exposing sensitive details in logs or not checking for window. ethereum before using it. Another is not testing on a testnet; practicing on Sepolia or another testnet lets you observe wallet prompts, confirmations, and receipts without mainnet risk. Design your UI to show pending, success, and failure states so users always know whether they need to retry, check their wallet, or wait for confirmations. These patterns reduce user anxiety and protect funds. Task

async function displayAccountInfo() {

    outputDiv.textContent += '
Wallet not connected.';

  }
}

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter you will learn how a JavaScript frontend talks to an Ethereum-compatible blockchain using ethers. js. We’ll build the fundamentals: installing the library, connecting to a browser wallet, reading a user’s address and balance, and sending signed transactions that require explicit user approval. This matters because the frontend is the point where users consent to cryptographic actions and pay gas. A reliable connection flow, clear error handling, and correct use of provider versus signer will protect users and avoid wasted transactions. For example, after connecting MetaMask your DApp will request accounts and then fetch the balance via the provider. When sending Ether, the signer prompts the wallet and the app uses tx. wait() to confirm mining. You’ll also see common pitfalls like not checking window. ethereum, mishandling user rejection, and revealing secret keys. By the end you should be able to wire up a simple DApp frontend, display account details automatically after connection, and safely trigger a small transaction on a testnet. Consider how users expect feedback and confirmations — that design decision affects both UX and security.

These objectives map to practical skills you will use when building a DApp frontend. First, you will set up a basic JavaScript project and install ethers. js so your app can import a provider and signer. This makes it possible to talk to Ethereum-compatible nodes without running your own node. Second, you will learn to connect a web application to a browser wallet using ethers. js, including requesting account access with eth_requestAccounts, and constructing a BrowserProvider. Third, you will retrieve account information such as the public address and balance by calling getAddress on a signer and getBalance on a provider, converting BigInt balances to human-readable ETH with formatEther. Finally, you will send simple Ether transactions from the frontend using parseEther, signer. sendTransaction, and tx. wait to confirm mining. Each objective focuses on both the A P I calls and the UX flow: how to prompt users, display results, and handle errors. Practice these steps on a testnet to avoid real cost and to see wallet prompts in action.

Alongside core A P I skills, you’ll practice user-focused flows and safety checks. First, detect whether window. ethereum exists and present a clear message when no wallet is installed; this prevents runtime errors and guides the user to install a wallet. Second, manage connection state and UI toggles so buttons for reading balances and sending transactions are enabled only when a signer is available. Third, handle user rejection of eth_requestAccounts and signer. sendTransaction by catching errors and informing the user rather than leaving the UI in a loading state. Fourth, respond to network and account changes via window. ethereum events to keep displayed data current and avoid sending transactions on the wrong network. These skills reduce failed transactions and improve trust. Practice these behaviors on a testnet, where you can safely observe prompts, rejections, and receipts without risking mainnet funds.

A predictable project setup is the first practical step. You will create a simple Node project, install ethers. js with npm, and serve static files so a browser extension like MetaMask can inject window. ethereum. The provided commands are standard: initialize a package. json, then install ethers. Running a lightweight static server helps avoid CORS and module import problems when using local modules in the browser. For example, run npx http-server to serve index. html. The index. html used in this chapter includes three buttons: connect wallet, get account info, and send a small amount of ETH. The H T M L is intentionally minimal, because the teaching focus is on wiring app. js with provider and signer. When adding ethers in a local environment you may import the ESM build from node_modules or bundle with your preferred bundler. For quick demos, the example uses the ES module path to ethers so the browser can import it directly. Practice this setup on a testnet so you can safely interact with wallet prompts without spending mainnet funds. Remember to check your node and npm versions so the module imports work correctly.

Two concepts you will use constantly are provider and signer. A provider is an abstraction that allows your DApp to read blockchain data: block numbers, balances, and logs. It does not sign transactions. A signer, by contrast, represents an account with the ability to sign transactions and messages; it typically wraps a user's wallet account once the user grants access. For example, provider. getBalance(address) queries the chain for a balance, whereas signer. sendTransaction(transaction) asks the wallet to sign and broadcast a state-changing transaction. Confusing these leads to common mistakes: calling sendTransaction on a provider does nothing, and trying to fetch private data from a signer is not its purpose. Practically, you create a BrowserProvider from window. ethereum, then call provider. getSigner() to obtain the signer for the connected account. This separation improves safety because read operations can be performed using public RPC providers like Infura when necessary, while signing always requires explicit user consent in their wallet. Remember: queries use the provider, state changes require the signer. Provider vs Signer means provider = read-only queries. signer = signing capability and sending transactions on behalf of the user.. In practical terms, understanding the roles: query vs sign. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Connecting a wallet follows a clear sequence that your app should implement and handle robustly. First, check for window. ethereum; if absent, instruct the user to install a compatible wallet. Second, call window. ethereum. request with the method eth_requestAccounts to prompt the user to connect. If the user approves, create a BrowserProvider from window. ethereum and obtain a signer via provider. getSigner(). Store provider and signer references, update the UI to show connected state, and enable actions like getting account info or sending transactions. Third, listen for relevant wallet events such as accountsChanged and chainChanged so the app can refresh data or prompt the user when the network changes. Always wrap the request call in try... catch to detect user rejection; a rejection typically yields an error code like 4001 and should be presented as an expected user action, not a fatal app error. This flow ensures clarity, reduces accidental transactions, and makes the app resilient to wallet state changes. Wallet connection flow means check window.ethereum, request accounts, create browserprovider and signer, update ui, and listen for account and chain events.. In practical terms, eth_requestaccounts, browserprovider, and signer lifecycle. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Let's walk through a practical connectWallet implementation. The code requests accounts, creates a BrowserProvider, and obtains a signer. It then updates the UI and attaches listeners for accountsChanged and chainChanged. When accountsChanged delivers an empty array, the wallet is disconnected; the app should clear provider and signer references and disable actions. When chainChanged occurs, the safest behavior is to reload or reinitialize provider and signer, because the network context has changed. This code pattern shows how to keep the app in sync with the wallet and avoid sending transactions to the wrong chain. Notice how the UI is toggled only after a successful connection, and how error handling writes friendly messages to an output area so users understand what happened. A common misconception is to assume provider and signer are always available after an initial connection; always verify their presence before every action to avoid runtime exceptions. In practical terms, practical connect flow with event listeners. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Reading account info is straightforward but requires the right objects. Use signer. getAddress() to obtain the connected public address. To read the Ether balance, call provider. getBalance(address). ethers. js returns balances as BigInts, so convert them to a human-friendly string using formatEther. In practice you will call displayAccountInfo right after establishing a signer so the user sees their address and balance immediately. Handle errors from provider. getBalance with try... catch and show clear messages for network issues. Also avoid assuming instantaneous balance updates; blockchain confirmations and pending transactions can change the displayed balance. After sending a transaction, refresh the balance by calling getBalance again once tx. wait resolves. A common mistake is displaying the BigInt directly or concatenating it without converting; always use formatEther for ETH values. Practically, the function displayAccountInfo should check that signer and userAddress are present, fetch the balance, format it, and append both address and formatted balance to the output area. Reading account address and balance means use signer.getaddress() for address; provider.getbalance(address) and ethers.formatether to convert bigint balances to eth strings.. In practical terms, using signer.getaddress and provider.getbalance with formatether. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Sending Ether requires you to construct a transaction object, request the user to sign it, and then wait for confirmation. There are two common ways a DApp connects to the chain: browser-injected providers like MetaMask and remote RPC providers like Infura, Alchemy, or QuickNode. Browser-injected providers allow user consent and signing through the wallet extension; they expose window. ethereum and are necessary for operations requiring the user’s key. RPC providers are node endpoints useful for read-only operations when you don’t need the user’s signature. A typical pattern is to use an RPC provider for heavy reads, caching, or server-side tasks, and use a BrowserProvider or injected provider only when you need to sign a transaction. Confusing these leads to UX problems: attempting to sign with an RPC provider will fail because it does not have access to a private key. On the other hand, relying exclusively on an injected provider for heavy traffic may be unreliable for some metrics or parallel requests. Plan your architecture accordingly: split read and write responsibilities based on whether a wallet signature is required. Reacting to wallet events preserves correctness in a DApp. Two events matter most: accountsChanged and chainChanged. accountsChanged fires when a user switches or disconnects accounts. If the array is empty, the user disconnected and you should clear any signer-related state and disable actions. If it contains a different address, update the stored userAddress and reinitialize the signer if necessary. chainChanged signals that the connected network changed; most apps choose to reload or reinitialize provider and signer because the chain context can change contract addresses, gas expectations, and balances. Always show a clear message so users understand why the app refreshed or why a button became disabled. Failure to handle these events leads to mistaken transactions or inconsistent UI. For example, if network mismatch is ignored, a user might unknowingly send testnet ETH while expecting mainnet behavior, or vice versa. Security and clear UX are essential in DApp frontends. First, never ask users for private keys or attempt to store them; wallets like MetaMask manage private keys securely. Second, warn users about insufficient gas and provide clear error messages when transactions fail due to funds or rejection. Third, detect network mismatches early and prevent state-changing actions when on the wrong chain. Fourth, handle promise rejections from eth_requestAccounts and signer. sendTransaction and present those rejections as possible user choices, not application failures.
